body:
Dance as a living cultural tradition

India has a rich variety of dance traditions reflecting its regional, religious, agricultural and social diversity. Folk and tribal dances express the experiences, beliefs, occupations and celebrations of communities. They are closely connected with festivals, agricultural seasons, marriages, religious worship and other important events in community life.

Many such traditions have been transmitted from one generation to another through observation, participation, oral instruction and community celebrations. Although their traditional forms remain important, folk dances also evolve and adapt to changing social conditions.

Major categories of Indian dance

CategoryPrincipal characteristicExamples
Classical danceEstablished systems of movement, expression and formal trainingBharatanatyam, Kathak, Odissi
Folk danceRegional and community traditions connected with social and cultural lifeGarba, Bhangra, Ghoomar
Tribal danceTraditions associated with particular tribal communities and their collective lifeBagurumba, Hojagiri, Popir
Ritual dancePerformance connected with religious worship or ceremonial observancesTheyyam, Garba
Dance-dramaCombination of dance, music, acting and storytellingChhau, Yakshagana

These categories are not mutually exclusive. For example, Garba is both a folk dance and a devotional practice. A tribal dance may also be performed as part of a harvest festival or religious ceremony. Folk and tribal dances can require considerable skill even though their systems of training differ from those of classical dances.

Why communities perform traditional dances

  • Agricultural celebrations: Bhangra of Punjab and Bihu of Assam express agricultural prosperity and seasonal joy.
  • Religious devotion: Garba of Gujarat is associated with the worship of feminine divine energy during Navratri.
  • Occupational activities: Tippani of Gujarat developed from collective labour, while Koli dances of Maharashtra reflect fishing activities.
  • Social occasions: Ghoomar of Rajasthan is performed during marriages and festive gatherings.
  • Martial traditions: Chhau of eastern India incorporates elements derived from traditional martial practices.

Regional identity and shared traditions

State-wise classification is useful for identifying dances, but cultural traditions do not always follow administrative boundaries. Communities living across neighbouring states may share related festivals, musical instruments and dance forms.

For example, Karma dance is practised in several states of eastern and central India, while Chhau has distinct regional styles in Odisha, Jharkhand and West Bengal. Therefore, the association of a dance with one state does not necessarily exclude its presence in another.

Classical and folk forms

The 8 commonly recognised Indian classical dance forms are Bharatanatyam, Kathak, Kathakali, Kuchipudi, Manipuri, Mohiniyattam, Odissi and Sattriya. Garba, Bihu, Bhangra and Chhau are not included in this conventional list of 8 classical forms.

Prelims focus

  • Folk dances express regional and community traditions.
  • Tribal dances are associated with particular tribal communities.
  • Harvest, marriage, religious worship and occupations are important contexts of traditional dances.
  • Chhau belongs to more than one state.
  • Trap: Folk, tribal and ritual classifications can overlap.

[References: NCERT, Our Pasts-II, Class 7, 2020-21 edition, Chapter 9: The Making of Regional Cultures, pp. 122-124; NCERT, Living Craft Traditions of India, Class 11, Chapter 10: Theatre Crafts, pp. 112-117; Centre for Cultural Resources and Training, Performing Arts; UNESCO, Garba of Gujarat and Chhau Dance element records. Online sources consulted 25 November 2026.]

title: Understanding Indian Folk and Tribal Dances

body:
Garba

Garba is a major devotional folk dance of Gujarat. It is particularly associated with Navratri, the festival of 9 nights dedicated to the worship of feminine divine power, or Shakti.

Traditionally, participants dance in a circle around a perforated earthen pot containing a lighted lamp or around a representation of the Mother Goddess. The illuminated pot symbolises life and divine energy. The circular movement expresses collective devotion and participation.

Traditional Garba is accompanied by devotional songs, rhythmic clapping and instruments such as the dhol and manjira. Although women have historically played a central role in Garba, contemporary celebrations involve participants of different genders and ages.

Religious and literary associations

Garba songs frequently praise Amba, Durga and other manifestations of the Mother Goddess. Gujarati devotional poetry has also contributed to the development of Garba and Garbi traditions.

Garba is performed not only during Navratri but also on certain other festive and religious occasions, including Sharad Purnima.

Garbi and the contribution of Dayaram

Garbi is a related Gujarati tradition of devotional song and dance. In traditional descriptions, Garbi is often associated with performances by men, while Garba is associated with women. However, this historical distinction is not an absolute rule governing contemporary performances.

The Gujarati devotional poet Dayaram is particularly associated with Garbi compositions expressing devotion to Krishna. His compositions frequently explore the emotional relationship between Krishna and his devotees.

Raas and Dandiya Raas

Raas is another important Gujarati folk dance tradition. Its devotional background is closely connected with the Raas Lila of Krishna and the Gopis.

Raas is generally performed in groups with rhythmic movement, songs and musical accompaniment. It is associated with festivals such as Navratri and Janmashtami.

Dandiya Raas is a variety of Raas in which dancers carry small wooden sticks called dandiyas. The rhythmic striking of these sticks is an important identifying feature.

Traditional costumes include the embroidered chaniya-choli worn by women and the kediyu with dhoti or other traditional lower garments worn by men.

Distinguishing the related traditions

FormPrincipal associationIdentifying feature
GarbaWorship of ShaktiCircular dance around a devotional centre
GarbiDevotional poetry and singingDayaram's Krishna-oriented compositions
RaasKrishna and Raas LilaRhythmic group dance
Dandiya RaasRaas tradition and festivalsWooden sticks

The Garba and Raas traditions frequently occur together during Navratri celebrations, but they should not be treated as identical forms. Wooden sticks are characteristic of Dandiya Raas rather than a compulsory feature of Garba.

UNESCO recognition of Garba

In 2023, Garba of Gujarat was inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity under Decision 18.COM 8.b.32.

The inscription recognises Garba as a living cultural practice involving devotion, music, dance, social participation and the transmission of cultural knowledge between generations.

Garba is recognised as intangible cultural heritage. The inscription does not designate a building, temple or geographical location as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Prelims focus

  • Garba: Navratri and worship of Shakti.
  • Traditional Garba centre: illuminated earthen pot or representation of the Mother Goddess.
  • Dayaram: devotional Garbi compositions associated with Krishna.
  • Raas: Krishna's Raas Lila tradition.
  • UNESCO inscription of Garba: 2023.
  • Trap: Dandiya sticks are not essential to every form of Garba.

[References: Gujarat State School Textbook Board, Social Science, Standard 10, Chapter 2: Cultural Heritage of India: Traditional Handicraft and Fine Arts, printed pp. 14-16, English chapter copy hosted by BYJU'S; UNESCO, Garba of Gujarat, nomination file 01962 and Decision 18.COM 8.b.32; District Kachchh, Government of Gujarat, Kachchh Folk Dances; Sahapedia, Ras Traditions of Gujarat. Online sources consulted 25 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Identifying Garba and Dandiya Raas.

title: Garba, Garbi and Raas of Gujarat

body:
Tippani: a dance originating in collective labour

Tippani is associated particularly with the Chorwad and Veraval region of Saurashtra. It developed from traditional construction work performed collectively by labouring communities, including Kolis.

A tippani is a wooden implement with a broad base traditionally used for pounding and compacting floors. Workers coordinated their movements with songs and rhythmic beats. Over time, these movements developed into a distinctive folk dance.

In contemporary performances, dancers use long wooden implements to produce a coordinated rhythm. Instruments such as the dhol, manjira and thali, or metal plate, may accompany the performance.

Occupational and regional forms of Raas

Different communities of Gujarat have developed their own varieties of Raas. Their movements, costumes, songs and props reflect their occupations and regional identities.

DanceCommunity or regionDistinctive association
Padhar RaasPadhar community, Nal Sarovar regionFishing, rowing and movements resembling waves
HudoBharwad pastoral communitiesPastoral life and energetic rhythmic movement
Mer RaasMer community, SaurashtraMartial and heroic traditions
Gajiyo RaasKachchhWomen dancing to the traditional Gajiyo folk song
Jat RaasJat Maldhari community, KachchhPastoral community tradition

Padhar dance is particularly distinctive because its movements represent activities associated with water and fishing. Sticks and manjiras are used in traditional performances.

Gof Gunthan

Gof Gunthan is a form of Gujarati group dance in which dancers carry ropes attached to a common central point. Their coordinated movements braid the ropes into a pattern and subsequently unbraid them.

The intertwined ropes are its principal identifying feature. Rhythmic music, including drum accompaniment, supports the collective performance.

Siddi Dhamal

Siddi Dhamal, also written as Sidi Dhamaal, belongs to the Siddi community of African ancestry in Gujarat. Jambur village in the Gir region is a well-known centre of Siddi cultural traditions.

The dance reflects the community's African cultural inheritance and religious traditions. Vigorous group movements, rhythmic singing, drumming and vocal calls are characteristic features. Traditional instruments include small drums and the mashira, a coconut-shell-based percussion instrument.

Peacock feathers and movements inspired by birds and animals may also appear in performances.

Dance traditions of tribal Gujarat

The tribal regions of eastern and southern Gujarat have numerous dances associated with agricultural life, marriages, festivals and collective celebrations. These traditions are especially prominent in districts such as Dang, Tapi, Narmada, Dahod and Chhota Udepur.

Dance or traditionAssociation
Dangi danceTribal communities of Dang
ChadoMovements inspired by birds and animals
Mali No ChaaloTribal dance tradition of Dang
Thakryo ChaaloTribal dance tradition of Dang
Rathwa danceRathwa tribal community
MerayoTraditional dance associated with Banaskantha

Group formations, locally composed songs and instruments such as drums, dholak, manjira and metal plates are common in several tribal traditions. The precise combination differs among communities.

Bhavai: an important distinction

Gujarat's Bhavai is principally a traditional form of folk theatre rather than a standalone folk dance. It combines acting, music, dialogue, dance and social satire.

Its traditional development is associated with Asait Thakar. Rajasthan also has a performance called Bhavai, but the Rajasthani form is particularly recognised for balancing vessels. The shared name should not lead to confusion between the 2 traditions.

Prelims focus

  • Tippani: Chorwad and Veraval, traditional floor-compacting implement.
  • Padhar: Nal Sarovar region and fishing-related movements.
  • Hudo: Bharwad pastoral communities.
  • Gof Gunthan: interweaving and unweaving ropes.
  • Siddi Dhamal: African-descended Siddi community, including Jambur.
  • Trap: Gujarat's Bhavai is folk theatre; Rajasthan's Bhavai is associated with balancing vessels.

[References: Gujarat State School Textbook Board, Social Science, Standard 10, Chapter 2: Cultural Heritage of India: Traditional Handicraft and Fine Arts, printed pp. 15-16, English chapter copy hosted by BYJU'S; Sahapedia, Ras Traditions of Gujarat; District Kachchh, Government of Gujarat, Kachchh Folk Dances; WRIKSH, Tippani Dance; Ministry of Tribal Affairs, Lok Sabha Starred Question 107, 11 December 2023, Annexure II; NCERT, Living Craft Traditions of India, Class 11, p. 113. Online sources consulted 25 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: The occupational origins of Tippani.

title: Regional and Tribal Dance Traditions of Gujarat

body:
Rajasthan

The folk dances of Rajasthan reflect royal and martial traditions, tribal customs, religious devotion and the occupations of its communities. Several forms can be identified through their distinctive costumes, props or musical instruments.

Ghoomar

Ghoomar is a traditional dance performed predominantly by women. It is associated with festive occasions and marriages. The dancers' circular movement causes their long skirts, or ghagras, to spread outward, producing its characteristic appearance.

Kalbelia

Kalbelia belongs to the Kalbelia community of Rajasthan, historically associated with snake charming. The movements of the dancers resemble the movements of snakes.

Women traditionally perform in flowing black skirts decorated with colourful embroidery. Men commonly provide musical accompaniment using instruments such as the poongi, a wind instrument, and the khanjari, a percussion instrument.

Kalbelia folk songs and dances of Rajasthan were inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2010.

Other important forms

DanceCommunity or regionIdentifying feature
GairBhil traditionHoli celebrations and rhythmic stick movements
GavariBhil communities of southern RajasthanSeasonal ritual dance-drama
BhavaiRajasthanBalancing multiple vessels
ChariGujjar community, Kishangarh regionBrass vessels carried on the head
Terah TaliKamad community13 cymbals associated with the body
Kachchhi GhodiShekhawati regionDecorated dummy horse
ChakriKanjar community, Hadoti regionRapid circular movement

Terah Tali, also called Teratali, derives its name from the traditional use of 13 manjiras. The performers are commonly seated and produce rhythm using cymbals attached to different parts of the body and held in their hands.

Maharashtra

Maharashtra's folk dance traditions include forms reflecting devotional worship, rural occupations, entertainment and physical exercise.

DanceAssociationFeature or accompaniment
LavaniFolk song and danceDholki and expressive singing
KoliFishing communitiesMovements representing rowing and fishing
Dhangari GajaDhangar shepherd communityPastoral and devotional traditions
LezimGroup exercise and celebrationsLezim, a jingling percussion implement
DindiDevotional traditionCollective religious singing and dancing

Lavani frequently forms part of Tamasha, the traditional folk theatre of Maharashtra. Lavani is a genre of song and dance, whereas Tamasha is a broader theatrical form combining music, dance, dialogue and entertainment.

Goa

Fugdi and Dhalo are well-known Goan folk dances traditionally performed by women. They are associated with community celebrations and religious or festive gatherings.

Other traditions include Kunbi dance, connected with the Kunbi community, and Goff, a folk dance associated with harvest celebrations.

Goan dance traditions reflect the state's diverse rural communities and religious customs.

Prelims focus

  • Kalbelia: Rajasthan, snake-like movements, poongi and UNESCO recognition in 2010.
  • Gair and Gavari: Bhil traditions of Rajasthan.
  • Terah Tali: Kamad community and manjiras.
  • Lavani: Maharashtra and dholki accompaniment.
  • Fugdi and Dhalo: traditional women's dances of Goa.
  • Trap: Kachchhi Ghodi is associated with Rajasthan, despite its name.

[References: Rajasthan Foundation, Dance Forms of Rajasthan; UNESCO, Kalbelia Folk Songs and Dances of Rajasthan, nomination file 00340 and Decision 5.COM 6.16; NCERT, Living Craft Traditions of India, Class 11, Chapter 10, pp. 113 and 121; SATHEE, IIT Kanpur, Folk Dances of India; Maharashtra Tourism information portal, Dances of Maharashtra; WRIKSH, Lavani; Directorate of Art and Culture, Government of Goa, Dhalo-Fugadi Festival; District Kushavati, Major Folk Traditions. Online sources consulted 25 November 2026.]
